full_judgment:
Mainur Reza Chowdhury, CJ: These civil appeals by the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House Chittagong and others are against the Single judgment and order passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 3252, 3077, 3099, 4148, 3226, 3230, 3228, 3050, 3051, 3108, 3683 and 3676 of 1997 and passed by another Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 3085, 3086, 3427, 3428, 3429, 3430, 3431, 3432, 3433, 3434, 3435, 3436, 3606, 4756 and 3283 of 1997. Both the Benches made the Rules absolute.

2. The High Court Division while issuing the Rule called upon the present petitioners to show cause as to why the orders passed by them on different dates directing for assessment of duties and taxes on the imported goods after fixing tariff value thereon by notification No. SRO No. 113 AIN/ 97/ 1705/Shulka dated 11-5-1997 withdrawing the scheme of CRF from the imported goods. At the time of issuing the Rules, the respondents were allowed to release their respective consignments by paying customs duties and other taxes on the basis of CRF and furnishing bank guarantee for the difference of the customs duty and other taxes on the basis of tariff value as per the impugned orders. The case of the respondents as writ petitioners was that they opened letters of credit when schedule 1 of the Pre-shipment Inspection of Goods Rules 1996 as notified by SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996 contained only 12 items to which CRF Certificates issued by pre-shipment inspection agencies were not to be applicable and the said 12 items did not include consignment of the respondents. Relying on the situation and facilities then prevailing the respondents opened letters of credit for import of various items not included in the aforementioned SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996. After inspection CRF Certificates were duly issued in terms of the provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 and the relevant Rules of 1996. Long after the letters of credit were opened relying on SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996, the aforesaid SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 was issued which among other items included the items imported by respondents in schedule 1 of the said 1996 Rules. Since the respondents opened the letters of credit long before SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 which came into effect from that date i.e. 11-5-1997 the respondents had acquired vested right to be assessed on the basis of the rules which existed when the letters of credit were opened by them and the present petitioners by issuing SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 could not take away the said vested right of the respondents in view of the principles as laid down in the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167, 48 DLR (AD) 199 and also the judgment dated 11-5-1998 passed by this Division in Civil Appeal Nos. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of 1995.

3. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the present petitioners submitted that in terms of the provisions of section 30 and 30A read with section 35(7) of the Customs Act 1969 the customs authority had power to fix the tariff value of the imported goods at the rate prevailing at the time of presentation of the Bill of Entry which in all the Rules were filed after 11-5-1997 and in any view of the matter the bar provided in section 30A of the Customs Act 1969, the order for fixation of the value of the consignment on the basis of tariff value fixed under section 16(7) of the Customs Act, calls for no interference. The High Court Division after considering the provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 and the fact that the respondents before us opened the letter of credit in terms of SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994 provided for the release of the goods on the basis of CRF Certificate was in operation and respondents got their goods inspected by the approved Pre-shipment Agency who after inspecting the goods issued CRF certificate in their favour as per provision of said SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994 and whereas SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 came into operation long after letters of credit were opened by the respondents it was of the view that the respondents before us had acquired vested right to have the customs duty assessed on their imported goods on the basis of CRF Certificates issued by PSI Agency and letter of credit opened in terms of SRO No. 316 Ain/94 /1568 /Shulka dated 31-12-1994. The SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 having been issued subsequent to the opening of the letters of credit the respondents vested right of assessment of customs duty of their imported goods as per SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994 and SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996 could not be taken away. The High Court Division found that their view was supported by the decisions given by this Division in the case of Collector of Customs vs A Hannan reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and also in the case of Collector of Customs vs Ahmed Hossain reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199 and Mostafizur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh case reported in 51 DLR (AD) 40. The High Court Division therefore held that the present petitioner acted illegally, arbitrarily and without lawful authority in refusing to release the imported goods on the basis of CRF Certificate issued by the pre-shipment inspection agency and that the SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 could not affect the vested right which accrued to the respondents pursuant to SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994 and SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996. Accordingly, the impugned orders refusing to accept CRF certificate and directing to fix the customs duties and other taxes on the imported goods on the basis of tariff value were declared to have been passed without any legal basis and of no legal effect. The consignments imported by the respondents were liable to be assessed on the basis of CRF certificate. The petitioners were directed to release the goods against bank guarantees to be furnished by the respondents.

4. This Division granted leave to appeal to consider the submission made by the appellants that the present cases being cases in which the imported goods have been excluded from purview of section 25A of the Customs Act and not being a case of withdrawal, reduction or exemption of duty under section 19 of the Customs Act the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 have no application in the present cases and the High Court Division committed error of law in making the Rules absolute relying on the aforesaid decisions. Leave was also given on the submission that the imported goods having been excluded from the purview of section 25A of the Customs Act, the value of imported goods is to be assessed in terms of section 25 in view of the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act and, as such, the High Court Division was wrong in holding that duty has to be paid on CRF value of the goods and that the cases were fully covered by the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149.

<u>5. Since in all these civil appeals common question of law and similar fact are involved the appeals were taken up together for hearing and are being disposed of by this single judgment. Admittedly, the respondents opened letters of credit prior to SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 and arranged for pre-shipment inspection of the imported goods by the approved pre-shipment agencies who after inspecting the imported goods issued clean report of finding (CRF) for the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of customs duties and other taxes in terms of section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 and the relevant Rules 1996 referred earlier. It also appears that the Customs Authority acknowledged the receipt of CRF Certificates but took the view that by SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 the CRF scheme was withdrawn in respect of the imported goods and accordingly, the provisions of CRF under section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 was not applicable to the goods imported by the respondents.</u>

6. It appears that in terms of section 25A read with section 219(1) of the aforesaid Customs Act, the Government issued SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996 framing the Pre-shipment Inspection of Goods Rules 1996 making provision for issuance of clean report of finding certificate (CRF) by approved pre-shipment inspection agencies and schedule 1 of the said Rules initially containing descriptions of only 12 items to which the CRF was not applicable. Subsequently, other items were included in the said list as it appears by SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997. The imported goods of the respondents were also included in schedule 1 and thereby imported consignments were excluded from the purview of the CRF scheme and relying on this SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 the petitioners by the impugned orders, refused to accept the CRF in respect of the imported goods of the respondents. We are now to examine whether by obtaining CRF certificate under provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act the respondent importers acquired vested right to be assessed at the rate of duty prevailing on the date of opening of the letters of credit similar to the right acquired under section 19 of the Customs Act as found by this Division in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and in 48 DLR (AD) 199 which could not be taken away by issuing another SRO subsequent to the date of opening of the letters of credit canceling or reducing the exemption as provided earlier. This Division in its judgment dated 10th May 1995 passed in Civil Appeal Nos. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of 1995 also applied the above principles as laid down in the above two cases of fixing or re-fixing of tariff value of the goods holding that the mode of valuation and or the rate of value as prevailing on the date of opening of the letter of credit, have to be taken into consideration while assessing customs duties and other taxes and the subsequent notification enhancing or fixing of tariff value cannot affect the vested right of the importer regarding fixation of the valuation of goods as per any notification or any matter prevailing at the time of opening of the letter of credit. Relying on the principles as laid down by this Division in the above cases the High Court Division was of the view that since in the present cases the respondents opened letters of credit in February/March 1997, the sub-sequent notification No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 could not affect the vested right of the respondents and the customs authority was under obligation to accept the CRF certificates. It noted that section 30A of the Customs Act 1969 came into effect from 1-7-1995 and present goods were imported subsequent to that date and that the sections 30A and 25A came into operation on the same date i.e. on 1-7-1995. But in section 30A there is no clause excluding the operation of section 25A and therefore, was of the view that the provisions of section 30A of the Customs Act was not applicable to the provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act relating to the CRF and the Rules framed and notifications issued thereunder.

7. This Division in the case Bangladesh vs Mizanur Rahman reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 took a different view on the question of acquiring vested right under notification of tariff prior to the opening of the letter of credit. It was, inter alia, held:

"That section 25(1) of the Act provides for determination of value of imported goods on the basis of normal price and sub-section (7) provides for fixing of tariff value by the Government by notification published in the official gazette for the purpose of levying of customs duty and as section 25(7) was not interpreted in 48 DLR (AD) 199 it is difficult to hold in the fact of sections 25(7) and 30 that earlier SRO will prevail when the letter of credit was opened and not the subsequent SRO when new tariff value was declared for levying customs duty. The argument of acquiring vested right may be tenable in case of exemption granted in a special circumstances as in Hannan's case but it is difficult to understand that normal importer would acquire vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value prevailing at the time of opening of letter of credit. The Government has the power to fix tariff value by publishing notification in the official gazette and this power has been vested in the Government under sub-section (7) of section 25 of the Act to fix tariff value of imported or exported goods by notification. As a matter of fact the then Attorney-General could not bring to our notice the distinguishing feature between Hannan's case and the case of Mustafizur Rahman, 51 DLR (AD) 40 which was a case under section 25(7) of the Act. As the present case is under section 25(7) of the Customs Act we are of the view that customs duty is payable by the importer-respondent on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of the bill of entry and not on the basis of invoice or tariff value in force at the time of opening of letter of credit. So the decision in 51 DLR (AD) 40 appears to us to be not correctly decided due to the failure of the then Attorney-General to point out the distinction between 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 on the one hand and the case of Mustafizur Rahman on the other. Even he failed to bring to our notice the case of Khairul Bashar vs Collector of Customs, 50 DLR 225 in which the High Court Division correctly noticed the distinction between exemption under section 19 of the Act and declaration of tariff value under section 25(7) of the Act and did not follow the ratio decidendi of 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 and held that importer acquires no vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value existing at the time of opening of letter of credit. We therefore, review our opinion expressed in that decision in 51 DLR (AD) 40 and hold that no vested right is acquired by the importer to pay sales tax and customs duty on the basis of tariff value declared by notification in force on the date of opening the letter of credit. The importer has to pay tax and duty on the basis of tariff value in force on the date on presentation of bill of entry."

8. We notice from the above judgment that this Division while making a distinction between Hannan's case (42 DLR) and Mustafizur Rahman Case (52 DLR) has observed that argument of acquiring vested right may be tenable in case of exemption granted in special circumstances as in Hannan's case. In that case this Division considered the contention of the appellants Collector of Customs that the notification under section 19 of the Customs Act is always subject to the provision of section 30 which would prevail over the notification issued under section 19 of the Customs Act. The facts in that case were that by a notification issued under SRO it was notified that in exercise of the powers conferred by section 19 of the Customs Act 1969 (IV of 1969) and section 4(1) of the Sales Tax Ordinance, 1982 (XVIII of 1982), the Government was pleased to exempt sugar from so much of customs duty and sales tax liable thereon as is in excess of 50% and 10% respectively, subject to the fulfillment of the terms and conditions specified in the Public Notice No. 28 (84-85) Import dated 3-10-1984, issued by the Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, Dhaka. The importer opened his letter of credit relying on the exemption which was withdrawn prior to the presentation of the bill of entry. The importer had relied upon vested right on credit under section 19 of the Customs Act. It was held by this Division in that case that the notification under section 19 was issued without any condition, limitation or restrictions excepting those which have been mentioned as "terms and conditions" therein. Several cases were discussed one being the case on Union of India vs Anglo Afghan Agencies AIR 1968 (SC) 718 in which it was inter alia, observed that even assuming that the provisions relating to the issue of Trade Notices offering inducement to the prospective exporters were in character executive, the Union Government and its officers were not entitled at their mere whim to ignore the promises made by the Government. It could not be said that the Textile Commissioner was the sole judge of the quantum of import licence to be granted to an exporter, and that the Courts were powerless to grant relief, if the promised import licence was not given to an exporter who had acted to his prejudice relying upon the representation. Hence, the persons aggrieved because of the failure to carry out the terms of the Scheme were entitled to seek resort to the Court and claim that the obligation imposed upon the Textile Commissioner by the Scheme be ordered to be carried out. After reviewing certain English cases the Supreme Court of India observed:

"That even though the case did not fall within the terms of section 115 of the Evidence Act, it was still open to a party who had acted on a representation made by the Government to claim that the Government shall be bound to carry out the promise made by it, even though the promise was not recorded in the form of a formal contract as required by Article 299 of the Constitution."

9. This Division therefore held that this case completely demolished the argument of the learned Additional Attorney-General that no formal contract was executed between the parties. It was taken into account that the respondent in Hannan's case had clearly acted upon the Government's assurance, and imported sugar, and because of such assurance the Government was estopped from denying such position. The respondent acting upon the solemn promise made by the appellant incurred huge expenditure and if the appellant was not held to its promise, the respondent would be put in a disadvantageous position and, therefore, the principle of promissory estoppel could be invoked in the case. Hannan's case was distinguished from Mizanur Rahman's case where this Division held that no such vested right acquired nor a promise could be implied to determine the normal value on the basis of the invoice of tariff value in force at the time of the letter of credit and therefore, customs duty was payable by the importer on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of the bill of entry.

10. The present case before us is on the question whether any vested right was created when the letters of credit were opened on the basis of CRF under section 25A of the Customs Act. Section 25A provides for pre-shipment inspection agencies and assessment on the basis of their certificates. Section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 as amended till 1-7-1995 which applies to the present case reads as follows:

"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act, the Government may, by notification in the official gazette, declare that the quality, quantity, price and customs classification of goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved pre-shipment inspection agency will be accepted as the basis for assessment.

Explanation—For the purpose of this section, 'price' shall mean the normal price determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 25."

After amendment in 1999 section 25A reads as follows:

(1)	For the purposes of this Act, the Government may, in the prescribed manner, appoint pre-shipment inspection agencies and determine the scope and manner of their certification and related matters.

(2)	The Government may, by notification in the official gazette, declare that the quality, quantity, price, description and customs classification of any goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by a pre-shipment inspection agency shall be accepted as the basis for assessment.

(3)	For the purpose of this section, 'price' means value of the goods determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 25.

11. We have seen that this Division in Mizanur Rahman's case has accepted that the argument of vested right may be tenable in specific circumstances as reduction or exemption of customs duty under section 19 of the Customs Act. It has been recognised by superior Courts of the sub-continent that specific assurance made by the Government may give rise to equitable protection under promissory estoppel. The question is whether a notification under section 25A of the Customs Act gives rise to a vested right and protection under promissory estoppel. Section 25A as amended till 1995 provides that the price verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved pre-shipment inspection agency will be accepted as the basis for assessment and the price verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved pre-shipment inspection agency will be accepted as the basis for assessment and the price under this section means the value of the goods determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 25. The respondents relying on the notification under this section acted to their detriment by having their goods inspected by inspectors appointed by the Government and by incurring expenses for such inspection. Would in such special circumstance of Government's assurance that the price so determined by the inspection would be accepted by them as the basis for assessment create a vested right? Would it be inequitable and unjust to allow the government to treat such inspection certificate as an idle exercise and a scrap of paper having no value at all? The promise of accepting the price having been made by the appellant under a law, should the Government be bound by such a promise when the other side has acted bonafide and to his detriment relying on that promise?

12. In the case of MP Sugar Mills vs State of UP reported in AIR 1979 SC 621 Justice Bhagwati has elaborately, inter alia, discussed the meaning of promissory estoppel and to what extent the parties including the State are bound by the principle of promissory estoppel. He has referred to and discussed several decisions of the English Courts on the subject. He has referred to Mr. Justice Denning as he then was, in High Trees case who observed: "that a promise intended to be binding, intended to be acted on and, in fact, acted on, is binding so far as its terms properly apply." Lord Denning added a qualification that though in the circumstances set out, the promise would undoubtedly be held by the courts to be binding on the party making it, not understanding that under the old common law it might be difficult to find any consideration for it, "the courts have not gone so far as to give a cause of action in damages for the breach of such a promise, but they have refused to allow the party making it to act inconsistently with it." Lord Denning also pointed out in Combe vs Combe, (1951) 2 KB 215 "Much as I am inclined to favour the principle stated in the High Trees' case, it is important that it should not be stretched too far, lest it should be endangered. That principle does not create new causes of action where none existed before. It only prevents a party from insisting upon his strict legal rights, when it would be unjust to allow him to enforce them, having regard to the dealings which have taken place between the parties..... ". He also referred to what Buckley, J said in the case of Beesly vs Hallwood Estates Ltd (1960) 2 All ER 314. "The doctrine may afford a defence against the enforcement or otherwise of enforceable rights: it cannot create a cause of action." Commenting on this observations Justice Bhagwati said:

"It is however, necessary to make it clear that though this doctrine has been called in various judgments and text books as promissory estoppel and it has been variously described as 'equitable estoppel', quasi estoppel and 'new estoppel, it is not really based on the principle of estoppel, but it is a doctrine evolved by equity in order to prevent injustice where a promise is made by a person knowing that it would be acted on by the person to whom it is made and in fact, it is so acted on and it is inequitable to allow the party making the promise to go back upon it. They are really promises, promises intended to be binding intended to be acted upon and in fact acted upon. It is an equitable principle evolved by the courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence."

13. Justice Bhagwati also discussed various cases against the Crown. He found that the doctrine of executive necessity propounded by Rowlatt, J., was, in fact, disapproved by Denning, J., as he then was, in Robertson vs Minister of Pensions (1949-1 KB 227) where the learned Judge said:

"The Crown cannot escape by saying that estoppels do not bind the Crown for that doctrine has long been exploded. Nor can the Crown escape by praying in aid the doctrine of executive necessity, that is, the doctrine that the Crown cannot bind itself so as to fetter its future executive action. " It is true that the decision of Denning, J., in this case was overruled by the House of Lords in Howell vs Falmouth Boat Construction Co Ltd 1951 (SC) 837 but that was on the ground that the doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked to "bar the Crown from enforcing a statutory prohibition or entitle the subject to maintain that there has been no breach of it." The decision of the House of Lords did not express any disapproval of the applicability of the doctrine of promissory estoppel against the Crown nor did it overrule the view taken by Denning, J., that the Crown cannot escape its obligation under the doctrine of promissory estoppel by 'praying in aid the doctrine of executive necessity'. The statement of the law by Denning, J., may, therefore, still be regarded as holding the field and it may be taken to be a judicially favoured view that the Crown is not immune from liability under the doctrine of promissory estoppel."

<u>14. Among the conclusions drawn by the Supreme Court of India in MP Sugar Mills vs State of UP are</u>

<u>"Doctrine of promissory estoppel has been variously called 'promissory estoppel', 'requisite estoppel', 'quasi estoppel' and 'new estoppel'. It is a principle evolved by equity to avoid injustice and though commonly named 'promissory estoppel', it is neither in the realm of contract nor in the realm of estoppel. The true principle of promissory estoppel seems to be that where one party has by his words or conduct made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or effect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowing or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it, if it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealings which have taken place between the parties, and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any preexisting relationship between the parties or not. The doctrine of promissory estoppel need not be inhibited by the same limitation as estoppel in the strict sense of the term. It is an equitable principle evolved by the courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence. There is no reason, logic or principle why promissory estoppel should also not be available as a cause of action, if necessary, to satisfy the equity."</u>

<u>15. Having discussed the relevant law and decisions with regard to vested right and promissory estoppel we are of the view that the position of the parties in the present case is like those arising out of promise made under section 19 of the Customs Act to exempt the import taxes and duties under special circumstances. The importers having acted on the promise made by the appellant under section 25A of the Act to accept the price determined by the government appointed inspectors and the appellants cannot go back on that promise as it was meant to be binding on them.</u>

<u>16. We may note here that section 30A of the Customs Act 1969 came into effect from 1-7-1995 and the present consignment were imported subsequent to that date. However it also appears that both section 30A and section 25A, came into operation on the same date i.e. on 1-7-1995 but in section 30A there is nothing to suggest that it excluded the operation of section 25A of the Customs Act. It is further noticed that section 25A (subsequently amended by F 16 of 1999 with effect from 1st July 1999) that at the relevant time the section contained non-obstantive clause like "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act which means that it included section 30A of the Customs Act. Therefore, section 25A would prevail over all other sections including sections 25(7) and section 30A of the Customs Act. The High Court Division observed that section 30A of the Customs Act is a fiscal law putting restrictions; it is liable to be interpreted restrictively. In view of the matter they were of the view that provision of section 30A of the Customs Act will not be applicable to the provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act and also to the Rule framed and notifications issued thereunder.</u>

<u>17. In the light of our discussion and observation of our discussion we are in agreement with the decision of the High Court Division that Notification No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 cannot affect vested rights of the respondents to be assessed on the basis of CRF price and the impugned orders passed in Writ Petition Nos. 3052, 3077, 3099, 4148, 3226, 3230, 3228, 3050, 3051, 3108, 3683 and 3676, of 1997 respectively on 27-5-1997, 25-5-1997 and 25-5-1997, 28-5-1997, 24-6-1997, 29-5-1997, 1-6-1997 and 25-5-1997, 28-5-1997, 27-5-1997, 26-5-1997, 24-5-1997, 16-6-1997 and 17-6-1997 refusing to accept CRF certificate and directing for fixing customs duty and other taxes on the imported goods on the basis of the tariff value, are declared to have been passed without any legal basis and are of no legal effect.</u>

All the appeals are dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.
